design_detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis, an update of McKetin et al. (2019) under that review's PROSPERO protocol (CRD42017081893), following PRISMA. Medline (PubMed in the abstract), EMBASE and PsycINFO searched May 2017 and updated July 2021; English-language, peer-reviewed human studies since 1950. Included: quantitative studies of methamphetamine or amphetamine use with depression or depressive symptoms measured by a validated scale or diagnostic tool, comparing levels of use and levels of depression (the last criterion added after the protocol). 14 studies: 11 cross-sectional and 3 longitudinal; 12 on any use and 2 on use disorder. Odds ratios pooled separately for unadjusted and adjusted estimates, by design and exposure level, with fixed or random effects chosen by the significance of Cochran's Q (MetaXL). Unmeasured confounding assessed with E-values and a five-item key-covariate checklist; no risk-of-bias tool.
can_establish: That, in the 14 eligible English-language studies to 2021, methamphetamine or amphetamine use was on average associated with modestly higher odds of depressive symptoms, more consistently in the three prospective cohorts than in the cross-sectional studies.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine causes depression or how large any effect is: the prospective evidence is three subpopulation cohorts with one or two adjusted estimates pooled, the use-disorder estimate is one cross-sectional twin study, confounding and reverse causation are not resolved by the E-value method as applied, and there are no dose–response or longitudinal use-disorder data.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level; participant numbers of the included studies are not reported in the main text. Included samples (Table 1): US national household survey (middle-aged and older community adults, by its title), US 8th- and 11th-grade students, Canadian secondary-school students followed from grade 10 to 11, South African high-school students, young people aged 14–29 in rural Thailand, community sentinel samples of people who use drugs (rural US stimulant users; Canadian LGBT people), HIV cohorts (Canadian gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men living with HIV; US HIV-positive and HIV-negative men who have sex with men), Cambodian transgender women, Nigerian commercial motorcyclists, US mothers recruited after birth in areas with high methamphetamine use, a US sample with methamphetamine use disorder, and male monozygotic twin pairs from the US military (Vietnam era). Most studies are North American.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Peer-reviewed quantitative studies; exposure methamphetamine or amphetamine use; outcome depression or depressive symptoms on a validated or diagnostic scale; usable data (e.g. odds ratio); cross-sectional, case-control, cohort or pre-trial RCT data. Added after the protocol: comparison groups had to differ in level of methamphetamine/amphetamine exposure (studies comparing methamphetamine with other drug use excluded) and in level of depression (studies comparing depression with another disorder excluded) (2.2).
sample.demographics: Not summarized; Table 1 gives setting and data years but no sample sizes, ages or sex distributions.
sample.attrition: Review level: 6606 records, 5821 unique screened, 5255 excluded, 566 full texts assessed, 14 included (3.1; Figure 1). Attrition within the three cohort studies is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English-only, peer-reviewed-only search with no reference-list, registry or grey-literature search; title and abstract screening by a single reviewer. Several samples are high-risk subpopulations (HIV cohorts, transgender women, LGBT people who use drugs, prenatal users), which the authors say may not generalize. No included study sampled people in treatment for methamphetamine use disorder over time, so the authors state the findings may not apply to treatment populations (Discussion, 6th paragraph; 6.1).

exposure.measurement: Self-report in all included studies as tabulated; use-disorder diagnosis by DSM-IV (past 18 months, Casaletto et al., 2015) or DSM-III (lifetime, Lin et al., 1996) (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Any use over varying windows: past 30 days, past 3 or 6 months, past year, lifetime, or daily/weekly use during pregnancy (Table 1). The authors state they had no data to analyse amount or frequency of use (Discussion, 6th paragraph; 6.1).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only through each study's own adjustment: other substance use is one of five key covariates (age, gender, employment, other substance use, pre-morbidity/comorbidity), and adjustment sets vary widely, from none to cannabis use alone to extensive lists (Table 3). The exposure includes amphetamine: one longitudinal study measured meth/amphetamine (speed) use (Briere et al., 2012, by its title).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; exposure and outcome were measured concurrently in the 11 cross-sectional studies.

comparison.controls: Within each study, people reporting no use (or less use) of methamphetamine/amphetamine, or without use disorder (Table 1).
comparison.matching: None at review level; the twin study compares co-twins within monozygotic pairs (Section 5.2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors note limited data on premorbid functioning, and that genetics, family history and life stressors were rarely measured (Discussion, 6th paragraph; 6.1). Only two longitudinal estimates adjusted for earlier depressive symptoms (Briere et al., 2012; Javanbakht et al., 2020) (Table 3).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison groups in sentinel drug-using samples used other drugs; in general-population and school samples other drug use varied and was adjusted for in some studies only (Table 3).

outcomes.instruments: Depressive symptom scales with varying thresholds: CES-D (continuous, ≥16, ≥22, ≥23), PHQ-9 (continuous, ≥5), HADS, BDI, BDI-II; diagnoses of major depressive disorder by DSM-IV criteria in a national survey, by SCID (Casaletto et al., 2015) and by the Diagnostic Interview Schedule for DSM-III (Lin et al., 1996) (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: All instruments are validated; thresholds differ (a PHQ-9 cut-off of 5 marks mild symptoms), so depression ranges from mild screening-positive symptoms to diagnosed major depression across studies. The authors could not analyse severity or major depressive disorder separately (6.1, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Depression as a binary outcome (depressed vs not, or higher vs lower level), effect measure odds ratio; unadjusted odds ratios were calculated by the reviewers from descriptive data where studies did not report them (2.4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; six pooled estimates (Table 2) plus one sensitivity analysis, without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; not reported for included studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled odds ratios (Table 2). Any use, cross-sectional: unadjusted 1.40 (95% CI 1.08–1.80), 10 estimates, random effects, Q 39.92, I² 77%; adjusted 1.66 (1.34–2.05), 4 estimates, fixed effect because Q 7.35 was not significant (editors' calculation: p≈0.06 on 3 df), I² 59%. Any use, longitudinal: unadjusted 2.05 (1.53–2.75), 2 estimates, I² 0%; adjusted 1.18 (1.08–1.28), 2 estimates, Q 1.76, I² 43% (the Results text gives 1.24, 1.14–1.34). Use disorder, cross-sectional: unadjusted 3.46 (2.04–5.89), 2 estimates, I² 0%; adjusted 2.80 (1.40–5.90), a single study. Sensitivity without the major-depression study: 1.37 (1.06–1.76). τ² and prediction intervals not reported. Editors' reproductions (inverse-variance on log odds ratios from printed intervals): the adjusted cross-sectional result is matched by DiMiceli recent use 2.60, Embry 1.33 (the value in the text, not in Table 3), Marshall 1.67 and Pluddemann 2.65 under fixed effect (1.66, 1.34–2.04; Q 7.40; I² 59%); a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model on the same four gives 1.85 (1.28–2.69). The two adjusted longitudinal estimates printed in Table 3 (Briere 1.60, 1.10–2.30; Javanbakht 1.50, 1.10–2.30) pool to 1.55 (1.19–2.01) with Q 0.06, so neither published longitudinal value can be reproduced from the paper's own study-level table.
analysis.covariates: Review-level adjustment not possible; included estimates adjusted for different covariate sets, from none to more than ten variables (Table 3). Five key covariates were used to grade confounding risk: age, gender, employment, other substance use, pre-morbidity/comorbidity (2.6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017081893, registered for the earlier, broader review that this paper updates (2.1). Deviation reported and explained: an inclusion criterion on exposure and outcome comparison groups was added beyond the protocol (2.2). Planned funnel plots, meta-regression and analyses by frequency of use and sample type were not done for lack of data (2.5; 6.1). Whether the E-value analysis was pre-specified is not stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: Study-level estimates in Table 3 do not always match those used or quoted elsewhere (see reporting issues). Forest plots are only in the supplementary file, which was not read.
analysis.power: Not assessed; most pooled estimates rest on 1–4 studies. Publication bias not assessed because there were too few estimates (2.5).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A modest positive association between any methamphetamine/amphetamine use and depressive symptoms (adjusted cross-sectional OR 1.66 from four estimates; adjusted longitudinal OR 1.18 from two cohorts, a value that does not match the paper's own study-level table), with individual cross-sectional studies split four positive and five null; a larger association for use disorder rests on two cross-sectional studies, one adjusted. No dose–response, severity or longitudinal use-disorder data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says people who use methamphetamine have higher risks of depression and that methamphetamine use, particularly use disorder, is a potential risk factor for depression, using risk language for odds ratios. It says the E-value analysis suggests very low to low risk of the associations being explained away by unmeasured confounding in most studies, but the E-values treat odds ratios as risk ratios although screening-positive depressive symptoms are common outcomes, and are computed for point estimates only: an unadjusted, non-significant estimate (Blazer and Wu, 3.42, 0.75–15.65) is classed as low risk. The twin study is said to provide strong evidence for causal inference and to show the association cannot be explained by genetics alone; its within-pair estimate is 7.0 (1.6–30.8) from one 1992 cohort, and the drug class of its use-disorder measure must be checked (its title concerns substance abuse/dependence generally). The Discussion also states that Colyer et al. reported significantly higher risk after adjusting for polydrug use, while the review itself extracted a null unadjusted estimate for that study. The abstract does hedge ("Based on limited data") and calls for causal-framework longitudinal studies.

timeline.event: Lin et al. Vietnam-era monozygotic twin study (included): use disorder associated with major depression within twin pairs, OR 7.0 (1.6–30.8)
McKetin et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use; this paper reports its pooled adjusted odds ratio for depression as 1.3 (1.2–1.4)
This update: 14 studies; adjusted ORs 1.66 cross-sectional and 1.18 longitudinal; E-value analysis added

replication.where_it_stands: Two overlapping syntheses by largely the same authors agree on a modest positive association (pooled adjusted odds ratios between about 1.2 and 1.7). Prospective evidence is three subpopulation cohorts; temporal order, dose–response and confounding by shared risk factors remain unresolved, and the authors call for causal-framework longitudinal studies.

funding.affiliations_note: University of Queensland (National Centre for Youth Substance Use Research; School of Psychology), National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre UNSW Sydney, Monash University Addiction Research Centre, Bahir Dar University. The senior author, who resolved full-text screening disagreements, co-authored one included study (Pluddemann et al., 2010) and the earlier review this paper updates. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure methamphetamine use (frequency and amount, toxicology-verified where possible) and depression by diagnostic interview repeatedly from before or near first use, including people with use disorder in treatment and community settings, analysed with methods that address reverse causation and time-varying confounding (within-person models or target-trial emulation); and a dose–response synthesis using consistent depression definitions.

domains.domain: Item 1: research question and inclusion criteria include population, exposure, comparator and outcome
Item 2 (critical): protocol established before the review
domains.note: PROSPERO protocol registered for the earlier review; the added comparison-group criterion is reported and justified; the E-value method is not stated as pre-specified.

domains.domain: Item 3: choice of study designs explained
domains.note: Observational designs included and cohort evidence explicitly prioritized (Introduction; 2.2).
Three databases with full strings (Table S3), language restriction justified, search within 24 months of publication; no reference-list, registry, expert or grey-literature search.
Title and abstract screening by one reviewer; full texts by two independent reviewers with a third for disagreements.
Four authors extracted; independent duplicate extraction is not stated.

domains.domain: Item 7 (critical): list of excluded studies with reasons
domains.note: 552 full texts excluded; no list in the main text, and none is mentioned among the supplementary items.

domains.domain: Item 8: included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Setting, data years, exposure and outcome definitions given; no sample sizes or demographics.

domains.domain: Item 9 (critical): satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: No risk-of-bias tool; only a covariate checklist and E-values for unmeasured confounding; selection bias and exposure and outcome measurement not assessed.

domains.domain: Item 10: funding sources of included studies reported
Item 11 (critical): appropriate methods for statistical combination
domains.note: Model chosen by significance of Q, giving a fixed-effect headline estimate despite I² 59% (random effects would give about 1.85, 1.28–2.69); the longitudinal pooled estimate cannot be reproduced from the study-level table; adjusted estimates with very different covariate sets pooled together.

domains.domain: Item 12: impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Adjusted and unadjusted estimates are separated, but no analysis by study quality.

domains.domain: Item 13 (critical): risk of bias accounted for when interpreting results
domains.note: Confounding, reverse causation, subpopulation samples and the limits of regression adjustment are discussed; the E-value interpretation overstates robustness.
Analyses stratified by design, exposure level and adjustment; mixed cross-sectional findings discussed.

domains.domain: Item 15 (critical): publication bias investigated and discussed
domains.note: Not assessed because of too few estimates; likely impact not discussed.

domains.domain: Item 16: conflicts of interest and funding of the review reported

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items fail: no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies, problematic meta-analytic methods (model selection by Q test with a fixed-effect headline estimate, and a longitudinal pooled estimate inconsistent with the study-level table), and no assessment of publication bias. Under AMSTAR 2 rules more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence. The registered protocol, multi-database search and E-value analysis are real strengths, and the direction of association is consistent with the earlier review by the same group; the pooled magnitudes, especially the longitudinal 1.18, should not be cited without checking against the primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 6606 records, 5821 unique titles and abstracts screened, 566 full texts assessed, 14 studies included: 11 cross-sectional and 3 longitudinal; 12 on any use and 2 on use disorder.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Study selection; 3.2 Study characteristics; Figure 1 (PRISMA flowchart, image)

key_findings.finding: Of the nine cross-sectional studies of any use, four reported a positive association (DiMiceli, Mburu, Pluddemann, Marshall) and five no association (Blazer and Wu, Colyer, Daniulaityte, Embry, Obadeji).
Any use, cross-sectional: unadjusted pooled OR 1.40 (95% CI 1.08–1.80; 10 estimates; random effects; Q 39.92; I² 77%); adjusted pooled OR 1.66 (1.34–2.05; 4 estimates; fixed effect; Q 7.35; I² 59%).
key_findings.note: Editors' reproduction: fixed effect on DiMiceli 2.60, Embry 1.33, Marshall 1.67 and Pluddemann 2.65 gives 1.66 (1.34–2.04), Q 7.40, I² 59%; DerSimonian–Laird random effects on the same estimates gives 1.85 (1.28–2.69).

key_findings.finding: Any use, longitudinal: unadjusted pooled OR 2.05 (1.53–2.75; 2 estimates; I² 0%); adjusted pooled OR 1.18 (1.08–1.28; 2 estimates; Q 1.76; I² 43%) in Table 2, the abstract and the Discussion.
key_findings.note: The Results text gives 1.24 (1.14–1.34) (3.4). The adjusted longitudinal estimates in Table 3 (Briere 1.60, 1.10–2.30; Javanbakht 1.50, 1.10–2.30) pool to about 1.55 (1.19–2.01) with Q 0.06 (editors' calculation), so the published value cannot be reproduced; check the forest plot in the supplement or the primary papers.

key_findings.finding: The three longitudinal studies: Canadian secondary-school students followed from grade 10 to 11, adjusted for earlier depressive symptoms and other substance use, OR 1.60 (1.10–2.30); US cohort of HIV-positive and HIV-negative men who have sex with men followed 3.7 years, adjusted for unemployment, antidepressant use, earlier depressive symptoms and HIV status, OR 1.50 (1.10–2.30); mothers with prenatal methamphetamine use followed 36 months, unadjusted, OR 1.90 (1.00–3.70).

Use disorder, cross-sectional: unadjusted pooled OR 3.46 (2.04–5.89; 2 studies; I² 0%); the only adjusted estimate is a single study, OR 2.80 (1.40–5.90) (Lin et al., 1996); no longitudinal study of use disorder met the criteria.
key_findings.note: The abstract reports 2.80 alongside pooled estimates without saying it comes from one study.

key_findings.finding: Twin study (Lin et al., 1996; male monozygotic pairs): index-twin OR 3.50 (1.79–6.80), adjusted for household income, education and combat experience 2.80 (1.40–5.90); within monozygotic pairs OR 7.0 (1.6–30.8), adjusted 5.8 (1.3–27.11).
Sensitivity analysis: removing the one study with a major-depressive-disorder outcome changed the unadjusted cross-sectional estimate from 1.40 (1.08–1.80) to 1.37 (1.06–1.76).

E-values (point estimates): 1.28 to 6.30 for cross-sectional estimates and 2.37 to 3.21 for longitudinal ones; classified with cut-offs of 1.68, 3.47 and 6.71 adjusted for whether a study controlled for at least half of five key covariates (age, gender, employment, other substance use, pre-morbidity/comorbidity). Table 3 grades 11 of 18 estimates as low or very low risk of unmeasured confounding.
key_findings.note: All printed E-values match the rare-outcome formula with odds ratios used as risk ratios (Obadeji excepted: 2.26 from its OR vs 2.56 printed). With the square-root conversion advised for common outcomes they would be smaller (e.g. Briere 1.84, Javanbakht 1.75, Lin 2.73, Pluddemann 2.64), and the E-value for the confidence limit is 1.00 for the nine estimates whose intervals include 1 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Depression definitions ranged from mild screening thresholds (PHQ-9 ≥5) through CES-D cut-offs of 16, 22 and 23 to diagnosed major depressive disorder (DSM-IV, SCID, DIS/DSM-III); exposure windows ranged from past 30 days to lifetime and prenatal use.
No data allowed analysis by amount or frequency of use, by sample type, by age group, or by depression severity; planned funnel plots and meta-regression were not done.
The earlier review that this paper updates reported a pooled adjusted OR for depression of 1.3 (1.2–1.4).

reporting_issues.issue: The adjusted longitudinal pooled OR is 1.18 (1.08–1.28) in the abstract, Table 2 and Discussion but 1.24 (1.14–1.34) in Results 3.4, and neither matches the two adjusted longitudinal estimates in Table 3 (1.60 and 1.50, which pool to about 1.55 with Q near 0, editors' calculation; the paper prints Q 1.76, I² 43%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's headline prospective estimate is unverifiable from its own tables; the encyclopedia should cite the individual cohort estimates instead until resolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says heterogeneity was significant for the adjusted cross-sectional estimates (3.3), but Table 2 marks Q 7.35 as non-significant (p≈0.06 on 3 df, editors' calculation), so under the authors' rule a fixed-effect model was used despite I² 59%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A random-effects model would give a larger estimate with a wider interval (about 1.85, 1.28–2.69); the headline 1.66 understates uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: Study-level values differ between places: Embry et al. appears as 1.33 (1.01–1.76) in 5.1.1 and in the pooled analysis but as grade-specific 1.28 (0.80–2.06) and 1.36 (0.96–1.93) in Table 3; Pluddemann et al. is 2.60 (1.60–4.20) in 5.1.1 and 2.65 (1.64–4.28) in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Values must be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion (7th paragraph) says Colyer et al. reported significantly higher depression risk after adjusting for polydrug use, but the review lists that study among those with no association (3.3) and extracted an unadjusted OR of 1.05 (0.92–1.19) (Table 3); the Discussion (4th paragraph) also cites Embry et al. among studies showing two-fold or higher odds, against its 1.28–1.36.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion overstates the consistency of the subpopulation and low-confounding-risk evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: E-value risk categories do not follow the stated cut-offs: DiMiceli lifetime (2.60) and recent use (4.64) are both graded low, which no single rule yields; Mburu at CES-D ≥23 (3.64, no covariates) is graded moderate where the stated rule gives low; Pluddemann (age and cannabis only) and Lin (income, education, combat, other substances) are graded very low, which requires adjustment for at least half of the five key covariates. The ≥50% cut-off list also leaves a gap between 1.6 and 1.69.
reporting_issues.consequence: The detailed rules are in Table S4, which was not read; as printed, the confounding-risk grades cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: E-values are computed for point estimates only, with odds ratios treated as risk ratios; non-significant estimates (e.g. Blazer and Wu 3.42, 0.75–15.65, unadjusted) are graded low risk of unmeasured confounding.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's and Discussion's reassurance about unmeasured confounding is weaker than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 10 cross-sectional unadjusted estimates under a column defined as number of studies, while nine cross-sectional any-use studies are listed; the abstract names PubMed but Methods name Medline; Table 1 calls a national household survey, a school survey and a study of people with use disorder general population-based cohorts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but study counts and sample types should be checked at source.

reporting_issues.issue: The use-disorder exposure in Lin et al. (1996) is labelled methamphetamine use disorder, while that paper's title concerns substance abuse/dependence in general; the review's eligibility accepted methamphetamine or amphetamine, and one cohort measured meth/amphetamine (speed) use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimates concern amphetamine-type stimulants broadly; the specific drug class in Lin et al. must be checked before the twin result is attributed to methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample sizes of the included studies are not reported in the main text, and the supplementary file (forest plots, eligibility, search strings, E-value rules) is a .docx download that was not opened.
reporting_issues.consequence: Weights, participant totals and the forest plots could not be checked.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/dar.13670 (all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, Figure 1 caption only, author contributions, acknowledgements, conflict statement, reference list; supplementary .docx not read)
